title: Notes of Ministry - 9 - August 1973

paragraphs.text: God loves to have Christ called attention to. There was that special time when the Father, in a most distinctive manner, Himself called attention to Christ, saying, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I have found my delight” (Matthew 3: 17). “Delight” is a strong word, in a positive sense. It is expressive of great depth of feeling. How the Father, God the Father, feels about His Son is a matter of the deepest, richest, affectionate feeling. I say this because there is much in our time that is admired by men, much to which men pay a certain tribute, much which may be rightly commended; but men’s admiration is a very shallow matter in comparison with God’s feelings as to Christ; they run very, very deep.

What are our feelings therefore as to Christ? What place has He with us? I do not just say, ‘What place has He in our affections?’—that must be the root of the matter—but what place has He in the fullest sense in what we speak of as our lives? The one would follow the other.

If in truth we love Jesus, if in truth we love God’s beloved Son, that very fact of itself will lead us to give Him a pre-eminent place in our lives; it must be so if in truth we love Him. If that shallowness which, alas, is in many respects a mark of the time in which we live amongst men, tends to mark ourselves, it might be that our lives are not yet lived with Christ in view.
If it is so it is to our great loss. What is said here as to a Lamb is to impress us with Christ in His absolute pre-eminence according to the place that God has given Him in His realm.

What John begins with in the first passage read introduces a stupendous statement, “Behold the Lamb of God, Who takes away the sin of the world”. It is the “sin of the world”; this is inclusive of my sin and yours. It is a part of this immense matter, “the sin of the world”.

Think of One being called attention to of whom it is said that He takes it away—There is one glorious Person to whom this stupendous matter is accredited. Would you leave such a Person out of your knowledge when He presents Himself to you, or maybe when someone else a little like John presents Him to you? Can you afford to pass by and take no notice of such a person as this? Do you not see your own case as part of the immense issue that is in mind here? “The sin of the world” reminds us of the root, that great power of sin which got hold of men. Does the power of sin, ever get hold of you? Were you able to refuse entrance to the power of sin? Were you able to say, ‘No, I shall not sin’, and follow what you resolved should be? Did the power of sin never get a grip in your soul? Would anyone here, however young, however old, dare to say it? Whatever merit a man might be supposed to have, whatever eminence he may have in the affairs of men, would he dare to say that the power of sin never got hold of him? If he did claim it he would not be right in claiming it. The scripture is plain, “All have sinned, and come short of the glory of God” (Romans 3: 23).

These remarks are made, not to point an accusing finger at any, but to point to Christ, to point to “the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world”. Think of that being said of One in manhood who came to John, as it seems in much the same manner that others came to John, to be baptised, just taking His place amongst men. What does that Person mean to you or to me? It is never recorded to be said of any other in the scripture. It could not be said of any other, in the scripture or in any writing or in any assertion of man. It could not be said of any other but Jesus. Therefore what is He to you? Could you forget Him? Could you leave Him out of account? Could you spurn His claims? Could you spurn His authority, spurn the pre-eminence that God has given Him?

This is John’s way of magnifying Christ, of presenting, as he loves to do, the full, immense scope and efficacy of the work of Christ. It is John’s way of appealing to us concerning the need in which we stand; he presents the full extent of the need to which our need belongs, and yet brings out that Jesus is the answer, not just to my need or yours, but to the whole matter of sin as it affects God. What it meant for God as men fell under the power of sin!

What it means to the heart of God to see thousands upon thousands of creatures, created by Him with intelligence above any other creature, carried away under the power of sin, rejecting Christ, refusing God, and going on regardless of what God will yet have to say in respect of this very matter—the sin of the world.

It affects your heart to think of it. How does God feel about it? But we have to come back to just our own responsible part in this matter. The responsibility of men in the widest way to God will yet be brought out when He comes in in judgment, judging the habitable earth in righteousness by the Man whom He has appointed, this same Jesus, who takes away the sin of the world.

Where do I stand in this? God would say to us in the word tonight, You have a responsibility, you are a responsible being, a responsible person; where do you stand as to the guilt of your sins? Where do you stand as to this matter of sin’s power in all its gravity as an offence to God in His rights, His glory? Where do you stand as to Jesus, “The Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world”? His own work has effected all that was justly necessary in the sight of God, that the taking away should be thoroughly established. It is the taking away that is emphasised here. We rightly speak, as the word is preached, of the responsibility of men to God, but here is One who takes away the sin of the world.

You say, How does God deal with my sins? He comes in to deal with my sin and yours in the provision He has made, in Christ’s death, for the whole of the guilt of my sins and yours to be purged away. There is no doubt about our guilt—the measure of it God knows. So the Lord Jesus went to the cross and suffered death. He suffered for sins, “the just for the unjust, that He might bring us to God” (1 Peter 3: 18). That is a beautiful scripture, indicating the extent of the efficacy of the work of Jesus, that He might bring us to God.

But what about the guilt? Shall you be brought to God in your guilt? That is not sufficient for God. One could be forgiven, and yet the guilt still be there. If you do something wrong and offend your parent or your schoolmaster or mistress—your parent will forgive you, the schoolteacher might forgive you, but in any case what has happened to the guilt? It is still there. I can recall things that I did which were wrong things, sinful things, when I was a very young child. You might say, Does the guilt remain? Thank God, no God has purged it away in One who was delivered for our offences and raised again for our justification. He went down into death as bearing my guilt. He came out of death. Did He bring my guilt out of death? Never! Did He bring the guilt of any out of death? Not any! It was settled, the whole question of sins and their guilt, finished for those who submit to the Lord, in that precious work of His in suffering and death. He “takes away the sin of the world”.

You see how this great principle of taking away is brought to bear on my case and your case. God has dealt with these things in the work of His Son. The cost in suffering?—stop and think of it! When I have finished and gone home, maybe, still think about the sufferings of Jesus. He suffered as here amongst men, feeling the awful condition through the sin into which men had come. He suffered in the garden, when He faced, in full communion with the Father, the immensity of the cup that He was yet to drink in suffering. He faced it, and was sustained in facing it, and never flinched in facing it, though it meant so much to Him. He suffered the cross itself, entire rejection by man, by Israel, by the rulers; He was just put on a cross. In that sense the world had finished with Him, as they speak. In that sense they have.
But things had not finished with Jesus when He was placed upon the cross. The deepest, the most profound suffering of all, was to follow in the three hours of His utter abandonment.

Why should Jesus be forsaken? Why is it that in the garden the perfection of communion was there, but on the cross He was forsaken? Because He bore just what was due to me as a sinner. And He died. Did men slay Him? No, not in the full, final sense. They put Him on the cross to die. They slew Him, in that sense. He laid down His life. He delivered up His spirit.

That was His matter, and He went into death for me and for you; He went the full length to which love could go, and it was love that went that way. It is a love that reaches right down these twenty centuries to this little company of persons in Bournemouth in 1973. Love was reaching right down as He went into death and met the whole sin question, and was raised out of death in the glory and might of resurrection power—a glorious Man out of death, beyond its power, having borne everything for you on this whole principle of, He “takes away the sin of the world”.

I believe John uses that expression because it embraces a great range of detail as to the work of Christ and what He will yet do in the sense of government and needed judgment; the whole matter is in His hands, but the principle is, He “takes away the sin of the world”. He comes into your history to take away all your guilt, to take away all that sin has done to your damage; to set you before God as God would have you before Him, that He may find His delight in you; to bring you now into the reality of peace towards God, real settled peace of soul. You say, Circumstances are difficult. Yes, they are, and they will be until the Lord comes, but peace of soul, a settled peace right in the depths of your being, is a settled peace governing everything because it is peace towards God. God will have us, so far as it depends upon us (Romans 12: 18), to be at peace with all men. It may not be that we can be—the scripture leaves room for that—but the point is that God would have this settled peace right deep down in our souls towards Him. The basis of it? The work of His Son. You cannot prepare peace; you cannot bring yourself into peace; you cannot work yourself up to a state of peace of soul. Some of us have tried—it is impossible. But God says, ‘I will do it’, on the principle of taking away that which could never allow peace. He has justly settled all in regard of His law, because all that God has done in Christ for your blessing is absolutely just and right, “so that he should be just, and justify him that is of the faith of Jesus” (Romans 3: 26).

So the word is, “Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world”. He is a real, glorious Person. One who has been into death and come out of death, and gone into that place of power and glory. God has exalted Jesus to His right hand, the place of power and supremacy, and it is the place of love too, the place in which the Father delights to have His Son. It is in this place that He calls your attention to Jesus at this time. Can you leave Him out of your life? God will never leave Him out, speaking with the deepest reverence, of His scheme of things. He has committed all things to be in His hand. “The Father loves the Son and has given all things to be in His hand” (John 3: 35), and yet there are still (Oh, the grief of it!) many, many, many souls of men who say, I do not want Him. Is there anyone here like that? Do you not want Him? What place is He to have, then? You might say, ‘Yes, I am not going to say I do not want Him’; but now the point is, what place are you going to give Him?

So the second word comes, “Behold the Lamb of God”; not now what He does, glorious as that is, but the One who does it, Jesus, the lowly Jesus, who went all the way for you in the love that fills His heart towards you still. What place will you give Him? Will you shut Him out? Would you try to give Him part of your life, part of your soul, part of your interest, part of your strength?’ I am impressed, looking back, with the fact that our committals have often been partial, which means in effect that they were not committals at all. “Behold the Lamb of God”—just take account of that Person under that title, that precious title, involving the sacrificial side; what He had gone into in the sacrifice of Himself is kept in view as the essential point of the whole situation. “The Lamb of God”—that is to get right into my heart and yours. He is still presented to us, though so great, so glorious, though in a place so wonderful, under the title “Lamb of God”, because sacrificially He met matters which no other could meet for you. That is always presented to your heart. It may not be stressed in any particular time, but it is always set there before you in Jesus, that He is God’s Lamb, the One who has effected in sacrifice that which meets your case, and no other provision could be made for your case save that which He has effected.

You say, ‘Am I to keep in view a Man in the glory?’ Yes, He is to govern things for you. Therefore God says, I will give you the Spirit; I will give you the gift of the Holy Spirit to sustain your occupation with Christ, to give you a link with the Man up there, the glorious Person of Jesus as He is and where He is He would say, I will give you the Spirit. It is not automatic, it is a matter of divine gift, but it is proposed in the glad tidings and it is normal, as Christ is received into the heart, that the gift of the Holy Spirit be received. It is the wondrous consummation and sustaining power of your link with Him up there.

Then you find yourself in company with others. “The two disciples heard him speaking and followed Jesus”. Not just one, but two. In principle it is a fellowship established, two persons who followed Jesus and walked in the same path, finding themselves in the same precious path, following Jesus. That is how you come into fellowship; you are alongside of others, thoroughly like-minded with you; but what you are first like-minded about is not in the affairs of our lives here, or men’s affairs, but the glory of the Person of God’s beloved Son and the claim that He has upon us, that we should follow Him. May this be the outcome in every one of us here, for His name’s sake.
P. van den Berg
Luke 1: 1–4; Hebrews 10: 21–22 to ‘faith’; 2 Peter 1: 16–19

I would like to say a word on certainty. It is important that we are assured, that we know where the way leads to; that we know why we are where we are at the moment; that we have an impression of the history of the testimony up to now and that, as to what is yet to come, we do not tread our path with uncertain step, as we have sung in our hymn. We should be fully assured as to the truth in the way it has come to us in these last days, and how it has been maintained by those who have gone before us. It is also important to have an impression of where things are now; where the Lord is as regards the testimony, and the prophetic character of this meeting where the Holy Spirit would announce what is coming. The word in Revelation 1: 4 is “from Him who is, and who was, and who is to come”, covering the whole scope of what has been, what is at the moment, and what is yet to come. There should be full assurance with us as to these things, beloved brethren, for if we are uncertain we do not know where we are going.

In the movements of Israel in the wilderness there was no uncertainty; the divine presence was there. As the cloud moved, they moved. There was priestly discernment as to the movements of the testimony, but not only discernment as to the way God moved but also a readiness to move on the part of the people, and sovereign leadership, Judah moving first, the royal side that is ready to move immediately when God moves. We read that “according to the commandment (lit. ‘mouth’) of Jehovah the children of Israel journeyed, and according to the commandment ‘mouth’) of Jehovah they remained encamped” Numbers 9: 18).

I think that is important, beloved brethren. The Lord says to Philadelphia, “Thou … hast kept my word” (Revelation 3: 8). It is not exactly the commandments, it is His word, what the Lord may say to us at any time. We can be assured that the line of the testimony, particularly in the revival, has come through, confirmed by the Lord’s own speaking, as Mary experienced at the Lord’s feet, and that the Lord in each phase of the testimony gave what was needed at that moment, and what the Lord said at every juncture was calculated to meet existing conditions at that moment. That does not invalidate what the Lord was saying many years ago, but His speaking then was in connection with the then prevailing conditions.

Therefore, in the day we are in, we may count on the Lord having a special word for us now. So the prophetic word is marked by certainty; it is no uncertain sound. In a prophetic meeting the trumpet is not to give an uncertain sound. The priest knew that the cloud had moved and when the silver trumpets were blown it was a definite sound and the whole camp moved. The line of the testimony will come through in the light of Paul’s ministry, and what marked Luke was that he was with Paul. Luke did not fall out by the way.

We read in the Acts how Luke came through in the shipwreck and in 2 Timothy 4: 11 Luke is with Paul. Paul says, “Luke alone is with me”. So we get a strengthening word in Luke’s gospel, a priestly word, for if the Lord speaks, it is priestly. The Lord is not only “the Word”, Luke 1: 2. He is also the Priest who will help us to go through in the light of that word and maintain us. Whatever weakness we may find in ourselves, the Lord is the One who feels and sympathises with us and He is able to save completely those who approach by Him to God, always living to intercede for us.

So in Luke the Lord is said to be carried up into heaven, which is not exactly Matthew’s presentation where the Lord is on our side in the testimony, which answers more to Judah. In Luke it is more the priestly side. Luke was prepared for small circumstances at the end. When Paul writes 2 Timothy he says, “All who are in Asia … have turned away from me” (2 Timothy 1: 15), but there are those who are available for the testimony and the line of the testimony goes through. It goes through in a man like Timothy, in faithful men. The line of the testimony will go through; it will go through in victory. That is what is represented in Judah, that God will never give up His thoughts. Paul says, “Remember Jesus Christ raised from among the dead, of the seed of David, according to my glad tidings” (2 Timothy 2: 8). That is the line of victory. At the end the Lord says, “I Jesus have sent mine angel to testify these things to you in the assemblies. I am the root and offspring of David, the bright and morning star” (Revelation 22: 16). So we have the line of David, the Lion which is of the tribe of Judah, and we see how the prophetic word is connected with the morning star. So Peter says, “We have the prophetic word made surer, to which ye do well taking heed (as to a lamp shining in an obscure place) until the day dawn and the morning star arise in your hearts”.

Well, that is to be noted here in Luke, where Christ is seen in the ascendency. God has visited His people, the dayspring from on high, and Luke speaks of the certainty of these things. That is important, beloved brethren, that we are perfectly assured as to what we stand for, whatever the outward circumstances may be. It is a question of faith. Faith does not go by externals, faith goes by things not visible but nevertheless real. Whatever is visible passes away, but faith is connected with an order of things that is not visible to the natural eye—but a living reality to the priestly eye, the priestly heart, “the eyes of your heart” (Ephesians 1: 18). So through faith we are in a victorious position, however small things may be at the end.
Paul could say, “I know whom I have believed, and am persuaded that he is able to keep for that day the deposit I have entrusted to him” (2 Timothy 1: 12). Paul was persuaded.

Whatever departure there might be in Asia or elsewhere, the distinctive line of ministry was seen in Paul, that elect vessel through whom the word of God was completed, the whole counsel of God. That is the distinctive line that will go through in the smallest circumstances, and there is no uncertainty; as we have sung—

‘It is not with uncertain step
We tread our desert way.’

In Luke we see how the Lord was led by the Spirit in the wilderness. I think that goes with the book of Numbers where the people moved in the wilderness, and the prophetic word is in the wilderness. The prophetic meeting is in the epistle to the Corinthians, where we have the assembly in the wilderness. That is where the prophetic word is. The woman in Revelation fled to the wilderness and the remnant of her seed has the testimony of Jesus—and “the spirit of prophecy is the testimony of Jesus” (Revelation 19: 10).

So it is important that we stand by the testimony, beloved brethren, however small the circumstances may be. Luke stood by the testimony as it was seen in Paul. Mark was restored and was serviceable to Paul for ministry. Timothy was to use diligence to come to Paul before winter. Then in 2 Timothy 4: 12 we have this special mission of Tychicus to Ephesus, the city, you might say, from which all that inhabited Asia heard the word of the Lord and where Paul had announced all the counsel of God—Ephesus! Paul would not give up Ephesus in his affections, in his feelings, and he sent Tychicus there.

What Paul must have felt in his heart that all in Asia had turned away from him! That would include Ephesus, and he sends Tychicus to Ephesus. So things were not out of hand in the end, Paul went on. Paul had combated the good combat and the Lord stood with him. It is important for us to know where we stand. There has been opportunity, beloved brethren, in the things that have happened in recent years, to go back, and many have used the opportunity to go an easier way, a different way. But what a privilege at such a time, at a time of crisis, to come out to the Lord, to come out to Him in faith and affection, in faithfulness to Him and to His testimony and to stand for what is so precious to His heart, the assembly, and the distinctive light brought out through Paul’s ministry.

When we come to the epistle to the Hebrews we see how everything stands immovable in Christ, the Son. There is no uncertainty. “Whatever promises of God there are, in him is the yea and the amen” (2 Corinthians 1: 20). So we have the Apostle and High Priest of our confession there, we might say, corresponding with the Word in Luke and the priesthood, available on our side to see us through, by the Spirit, in the light of Paul’s ministry. It is important to have a sense of the presence of the Holy Spirit, a divine Person. The Son is presented in Hebrews 1. In chapter 2 He is on our side. In chapter 3 He is the Apostle and High Priest of our confession, followed by this word of warning, “whose house are we, if indeed we hold fast the boldness and the boast of hope firm to the end” (Hebrews 3: 6). The practical maintenance of the testimony depends on our perseverance, holding fast, not turning to the right or to the left (Joshua 1: 7).

So it is a question of certainty; that we know whom we have believed, whom we follow; where things were in 1970, and in the sorrow of 1972, and to know where things are now. It is not a question of numbers; it is a question of what is available in a living way for the testimony, in the light of the whole assembly. What is maintained here for the Lord is maintained on behalf of the whole assembly. We would desire that all the saints were available to us. We shall be together at the rapture. That will be the last trump, when we shall meet the Lord in the air. We have the movements of the testimony now, and there are those moving at the sound of the silver trumpets. The Lord is entitled to have that. The silver speaks of redemption; we have been bought with a price; God is entitled to have us (1 Corinthians 6: 20).

So in Hebrews we see things established in the Lord. There is a kingdom not to be shaken; things stand secure on the divine side. Let us never have any doubt as to what is established on the divine side. The firm foundation of God stands. “God is faithful, by whom ye have been called into the fellowship of his son Jesus Christ our Lord” (1 Corinthians 1: 9). There is no breakdown there. Every saint is called into the fellowship of God’s Son. Every true saint is part of Christ’s body, and there is no breakdown there. The unity of the Spirit has net broken down. All the departure on our side has not altered the fact that there is one body and one Spirit. God’s truth stands, but the point for us is to stand in the light of what is immovable from the divine side. The apostle could say, “Wherefore let us, receiving a kingdom not to be shaken, have grace by which let us serve God acceptably with reverence and fear” (Hebrews 12: 29). Faith links on with that.

So we have this access. “Having therefore, brethren, boldness for entering into the holy of holies by the blood of Jesus, the new and living way which he has dedicated for us through the veil, that is, his flesh” (Hebrews 10: 19, 20). Oh, what stability that gives us, to have an anchor within the veil, an anchor that will not slip! If a ship is anchored and the anchor slips the whole ship goes with it. But we have an anchor where Jesus is entered as Forerunner within the veil. Everything is certain and secure there. Then it says, “Having a great priest over the house of God”. Oh, what a Priest He is—the greatness of the

Person of the Lord Jesus! Not only is He the One that built the house, as God, but He is Priest over the house, and He maintains the order of that house inasmuch as it is His house. Let us be assured that whatever departure there may be, whatever the state of things in the great house may be, the house of God is the house of God, and the principles governing that house are not subject to change, even though there be a great house.

Then the apostle says, “Let us approach with a true heart, in full assurance of faith, sprinkled as to our hearts from a wicked conscience, and washed as to our body with pure water. Let us hold fast the confession of the hope unwavering, (for he is faithful who has promised)”. What a point that is, that He is faithful even when we are unfaithful! The Lord is faithful and the Lord in His faithfulness will see the testimony through. Our hearts go out to our brethren not now available to us, as we say, but the Lord is faithful and God is faithful “by whom ye have been called into the fellowship of His Son” .God in His faithfulness stands by His truth. He stands by the principles, and may the Lord grant us grace to hold fast the confession of the hope unwavering. May we be characterised by drawing near; not by departing from these divine utterances, but making use freely of the throne of grace.

We have a kingdom that is immovable, with an immovable throne, and we are able to draw near in full assurance of faith knowing that our God is the living God, the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. He is the God of the living, the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the God who will see His thoughts through, right to the end. He is faithful; His gifts and calling are not subject to repentance.

God does not go back on His own thoughts; He never gives them up. The purpose of God from before the ages of time stands; it is as sure today as it was at Pentecost, and it is for us, at the close of this dispensation, to go through in the light of that which marked the beginning of it.

So in Peter we have one who was with the Lord from the beginning and who was about to depart. Peter wants to strengthen us in the things that are immovable. He tells us of the certainty of the things which we have come to. “For we have not made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, following cleverly imagined fables, but having been eyewitnesses of his majesty” (2 Peter 1: 16). What a voice he heard on the mount, “This is my beloved Son; hear him” (Mark 9: 7). There was no trace of uncertainty with Peter. In him we have a man who had come to the certainty of things, however unsteadfast things might once have been in himself, he came through to the rock, that which is immovable.

Christ Himself is the Rock, but the work of God in Peter was kindred to it, and the work of God in the saints is beyond breakdown; it is connected with the Rock Himself. The living stones, as Peter says, are being built up a spiritual house.

So we see how he cherished these things in his soul when he was about to put off his tabernacle. He is concerned that if anyone speak it is “as oracles of God” and “if any one minister—as of strength which God supplies” (1 Peter 4: 11). He brings out the Lord’s sufferings, His glory, and judgment beginning from the house of God. And as he comes to the end he recalls such a voice uttered from heaven when with Him on the holy mount. That never left Peter, the certainty of the things on that mountain. Peter got adjusted; it was not to be Moses, not Elias, but Christ, “This is my beloved Son—hear him”. That is the certainty of what Peter was connected with. Then he refers to “the prophetic word made surer, to which we do well taking heed (as to a lamp shining in an obscure place) until the day dawn and the morning star arise in your hearts”.

Well, the coming of the Lord is near. Soon we shall see the Lord. We shall see Him face to face. We love His appearing. The Lord will take His own away. But then the Lord will appear publicly with His own. Paul speaks of those who love His appearing. It is like the day dawn, but before the day dawn we have the morning star. The morning star is the Lord Jesus cherished during the night of His rejection in the affections of His own. He is in the ascendency, the morning star is arising in the hearts of His own. The Lord’s coming is at hand. We shall soon see Him. With this hope in our hearts we shall not by moved. The Thessalonians were moved because they were not in the gain of the light of the morning star.
The apostle brings it out in 1 Thessalonians 4 that the Lord Jesus will come first for His own, and that His own will meet Him in the air, before He will appear publicly with His own.

Well, beloved brethren, may our hearts, in the certainty of these things, continue steadfastly that we may with purpose of heart follow the Lord, “looking stedfastly on Jesus, the leader and completer of faith”, and holding the beginning of the assurance firm to the all, for His name’s sake.
Rijswijk

articles.title: THE DESIRES OF THE SAINTS, AND OF CHRIST
articles.author: F. N. Stickland

paragraphs.text: Two things have prompted me to think of these scriptures; one was in the hymn, which spoke about beholding the beauty of the Lord, the other was our brother’s prayer in which he said that God is always speaking to us and that it is on the principle of God speaking that we live.

We live on the principle of every word that is coming out of God’s mouth. I think, beloved brethren, that one thing the blessed God is intent upon is that we might develop our links with Jesus, become more acquainted with Him, and be able to speak more of His perfections and beauties.

There is nobody like Jesus to attract and hold the heart of every lover of His throughout time and eternity. What a beautiful Man He is! Not a flaw in Jesus! And this psalmist, David, in this psalm says, “One thing have I asked of Jehovah”. I think this would be the fruit or outcome of listening to what God has to say, because He is intent, and the Spirit is intent, on magnifying Jesus and making Him greater and more precious to every one of our hearts. He is worthy of it!

I love to look upon the faces of the beloved brethren here, many of whom I have never seen before, but the very fact that we are here shows that we have some interest, some real, deep interest, in the things of the Lord Jesus Christ. “All seek their own things, not the things of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 2: 21). Paul says, but through grace and mercy we are among those who delight to seek His things and be found developing in our acquaintance with Him—and the more we get to know Him the more we shall become like Him.

I believe that is one of the intentions of the blessed God, that we should value the qualities of the manhood of Jesus, so perfect and precious under His eye—for there was nothing about the life of Jesus that had to be adjusted. He never took a step that had to be recalled or re-trodden. He never said a word that had to be withdrawn, and He never did an action that had to be undone. What perfection! Does it not do us good, beloved brethren, to bathe our souls in the contemplation of the preciousness and the beauty of Jesus? It is said of some that when they see Him there is no beauty in Him that they should desire Him (Isaiah 53: 2). But I believe that God is intent on securing us so that we shall not be happy, we shall not rest, until our affections are really bound up, knit as one together, on the basis of our affection for Jesus and our links with Him.

“One thing have I asked”; what is the governing motive of our life, dear brethren? You know, we must get our priorities right. This dear man, David, the sweet psalmist of Israel, said, “One thing have I asked … that will I seek after; that I may dwell in the house of Jehovah all the days of my life, to behold the beauty of Jehovah, and to inquire of him in his temple”. It is the way we develop and grow, inquiring in His temple, the place where light is, where teaching is, where instruction is, not to say the blessedness and the protection of the sphere where the dominant Man is Jesus, and Jesus only.

Let us develop, beloved, let us set ourselves to develop in our appreciation and understanding of the beauty of Jesus, the beauty of Jehovah. It is not His mighty power exactly, not His authority, though He has all that. The Father loves the Son because of the beauty He sees in Him. He has committed everything into His hand. What more competent hands could there be than the hands of Jesus? But it is His beauty that is going to hold us through every test and every vicissitude of the testimony. We have had enough of them in our day, have we not? It may be that there will be further tests—who can say? In one sense the course of the testimony is a continuous test, a test as to whether we are going to be loyal, remain loyal and faithful to the One who amidst unfaithfulness was always faithful to His God and displayed the qualities and perfections and beauties that ever, if we may speak reverently, ravished the heart of God Himself.

In Psalm 45 it is a remarkable thing that it says that He, that is the Lord, will desire our beauty. Now that raises a question as to how we look upon the saints. Do we see beauties and qualities amongst the brethren? I know this is typical of the assembly, the bride, the king’s daughter all glorious within. A lovely psalm this, you know, and many here could unfold much better than I can what is contained in it; but what arrests me at the moment—I think the Spirit has just put it into my heart afresh—is that the Lard Jesus desires the beauty of the assembly. What is the assembly but the product of divine handiwork? There are suggestions of the embroidered garments, of course, which may have something to do with what we contribute. You know it is going to be given to the bride, in the day quickly to come, to be arrayed in the robe which is the righteousnesses of the saints, that embroidered garment. But here the suggestion is “her clothing is of wrought gold” and then again it says, “she shall be brought unto the king in raiment of embroidery”—but, you know, the bride does not eye her garment, she eyes her bridegroom’s face. But here it is the bridegroom looking upon the bride for her beauty.

I believe, beloved brethren, we would be encouraged that there are features amongst us that are beautiful under the eye of Christ, and He desires that beauty, He longs for it, He wants to see it developed, He wants to have such a vessel united to Him. We have experiences of this following the Supper, the bride united to the Bridegroom—a wonderful thing. One of the features would be that the King, the Bridegroom, desires her beauty. It is a wonderful thing that the production of these qualities and beautiful features is going on now. We can contribute to it; we can afford an atmosphere in which what is capable of being developed on this line can go on, the Spirit having His free way because He loves to adorn and beautify the assembly for the heart of His Master, the blessed, glorious Bridegroom. Well, may our hearts be encouraged and seek to be helped further on these lines, for His name’s sake.
Brooklyn
